scenes.narration: Meta is worth about one point six four trillion dollars. That's six hundred and forty-one dollars and thirty-nine cents a share at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six, times about two point six billion shares. And last quarter, for the first time in years, its free cash flow, as Meta defines it, was negative two point one billion dollars.

That's not because the business is shrinking. Ad revenue grew twenty-six percent. It's because Meta is spending about forty-five percent of everything it sells on data centers and servers. And instead of buying back stock, it just lined up about fifty-six billion dollars of new money in two weeks, by our count.
So what is this price actually betting on? What has to happen for all that spending to pay off? And what could break the story?
In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Meta reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Meta's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.narration: Over the last twelve months, Meta brought in about two hundred and forty-two billion dollars, and ninety-seven and a half percent of it came from advertising. Meta's own filing says it plainly. Substantially all of its revenue comes from marketers advertising on Facebook and Instagram. And those marketers don't sign long term contracts.

There are two engines. The Family of Apps, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, earned an operating margin of about fifty-two percent in twenty twenty-five. Reality Labs, the headsets and glasses, brings in very little and lost about nineteen billion dollars that year. One engine pays for the other.

The money machine itself is simple. In the third quarter, Meta showed ten percent more ads than a year earlier, and charged fourteen percent more per ad, mostly because its targeting and measurement got better. About three point six four billion people use at least one of its apps every day. More ads, at higher prices, to almost everyone online.

Where does that money come from? The United States and Canada bring in about thirty-nine percent of revenue. Europe, twenty-three percent. Asia Pacific, about twenty-seven percent. The rest of the world, eleven percent. And the machine is getting leaner. Meta's headcount is down fifteen percent from a year ago, to about sixty-seven thousand people. Almost all the spending, eighty-nine percent of costs, goes into the apps, and the rest into the headsets and glasses lab.

Let me draw the machine. Here is the Family of Apps, the big engine. Here is Reality Labs, the small one. Here is advertising, feeding the big engine. And this arrow is the cash the big engine sends over to keep the small one running.

scenes.narration: An ad machine that good throws off a lot of cash. So where did it go?

scenes.narration: Operating cash flow over the last twelve months was about one hundred and thirty-three billion dollars. Net income was about seventy-five billion dollars, though that includes a big tax benefit and billions in legal charges. Then capex, including finance leases, took about one hundred and eight billion dollars. Free cash flow, by Meta's definition, was about twenty-five billion dollars.

And the latest quarter went below zero. The third quarter also carried a nine point eight nine billion dollars charge for the settlement with state attorneys general. Including it, the Family of Apps margin fell to about twenty-seven percent. Without it, by our math, it would have been about forty-two percent.

So Meta changed direction on capital. In twenty twenty-five it bought back about twenty-six billion dollars of stock. This year, none. Instead, in two weeks it committed twelve and a half billion dollars of convertible preferred, a forward sale of new shares worth about twenty-nine billion dollars, and fifteen billion dollars of bonds. The share count is now rising, not falling.

And the bills are already signed. Meta lists about four hundred and fifty-five billion dollars of non cancelable contractual commitments. About about forty-six billion dollars is due this year, and about one hundred and twenty-one billion dollars next year. At the end of September, it held about eighty-two billion dollars of cash and securities, against about eighty-four billion dollars of debt. So for the first time in years, the balance sheet is roughly even, and with no buybacks, the share count rose about about one percent in nine months.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the big question. At one point six trillion dollars, what are you paying for?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the last twelve months. Price to earnings, about twenty-two times, though one offs push that number around in both directions. Free cash flow yield, about one and a half percent. Operating cash flow yield, about eight percent. That gap is the whole story. The cash is there. The capex is eating it.

So for a company in a building spree, we use a proxy. We take operating cash and subtract depreciation and amortization, about about twenty-five billion dollars a year, as a rough stand-in for the spending needed just to keep things running. That leaves about one hundred and eight billion dollars, a yield of about six and a half percent. It assumes capex eventually falls back toward that level.

Now let's run it backwards. What growth in that cash, for ten years, makes today's price work, before slowing to three percent? With an eight percent discount rate, about zero. With ten percent, about three and a half percent. But on today's actual free cash flow, the answer jumps to between about eighteen percent and about twenty-three percent a year.

So the bet is the capex. One more lens, our rough illustration. If Meta keeps spending at today's pace, every dollar of capex has to add about about ten cents to about sixteen cents of extra operating cash every year, within a decade, for the price to make sense. Less than Microsoft needs, by the same math, but Meta's spending is still climbing.

scenes.narration: Number one, ads keep compounding. Price per ad up fourteen percent, impressions up ten percent. For this quarter, the C F O guided revenue of seventy-three to seventy-six billion dollars, and says the A I work should help sustain strong revenue growth throughout next year. That's the engine everything else depends on.

Number two, capex turns back into cash. Meta guides twenty twenty-six capex of one hundred and thirty-five to one hundred and forty-five billion dollars. By our math, that implies about forty-nine to fifty-nine billion dollars in this quarter alone, far above the last one. And it has four hundred and fifty-four billion dollars of future commitments on the books, with about one hundred and twenty-one billion dollars due next year.

Number three, the core margin holds once the legal charges stop. It was about fifty-two percent last year, and about about forty-two percent last quarter before the settlement charge. Depreciation from all that new equipment is already rising fast, so this margin will be under pressure.

And number four, Reality Labs shrinks its losses as promised. The C F O expects eighteen to nineteen billion dollars this year, and around fifteen billion dollars next year. Every billion saved there is a billion that can go into A I instead.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one is the courts. A New Mexico court imposed a civil penalty of twenty-five billion dollars, with fifteen percent post judgment interest. Meta says it has accrued an amount and will appeal, but doesn't say how much. The settlement with state attorneys general could cost up to about eighteen point six billion dollars. Legal accruals now total about twenty billion dollars.

And the youth safety cases aren't over. The settlement with the states is paid over ten years, with about twelve point seven billion dollars in installments, plus about about five point three billion dollars more that only comes due if rivals like YouTube and TikTok adopt similar protections. Lawyers for more than two hundred thousand people have sent mass arbitration demands. The next school district trial is set for February. And the District of Columbia is seeking up to one point seven billion dollars in penalties. Plaintiffs have claimed damages above a trillion dollars in some cases, but that's their number, not an estimate.

Risk two is Europe, about about twenty-three percent of revenue. Meta is appealing a fine over its pay or consent model, and warns that further changes could be imposed, with a significant impact on its European business.

Risk three is the spending itself, and control. Meta's filing says that if its investments aren't successful longer term, the business could be harmed, and notes shifting public sentiment toward data centers. It depends on Mark Zuckerberg, and the new non voting shares could extend his majority of the votes for longer.

And the upside the price might not fully include. WhatsApp paid messaging and subscriptions grew fifty-nine percent last quarter, though it's still small, about about four billion dollars a year. Meta has launched Muse, an agentic A I it plans to scale, and A I glasses are selling. None of that comes with a forecast, so we won't size it.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected around late January twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, fourth quarter revenue against the seventy-three to seventy-six billion dollar guide. Two, capex, and the first outlook for next year, which decide whether free cash flow climbs back above zero. Three, legal accruals and the core margin. And one note for next time. Meta's new share dividend works like a two for one split, so the share count roughly doubles.
That's Meta, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
